utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning. Please be seated. May we please hear the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. This is case number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And the appearances, please, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Nicholas Koumjian, Ann Sutherland, and Ruth Karper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Branko Lukic and John Ostojic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Before we start, some remarks. First, it is to indicate that I learned from the Registry that the parties and the Bench will be provided with CD-ROMs where we have in one compilation all the transcripts and, including the closing arguments of the parties available as soon as possible and as soon as practicable. I think it would be a good idea if all the parties could indicate to the Registry how many copies you would need for your preparation. I don't know what will be the time necessary for the closing arguments to be given by the Defence. They have the time they need, no doubt. But I regard it in the moment as premature already to decide now whether or not it will be necessary to have rebuttal, rejoinder, questions by the Judges, and so on, tomorrow. One other more substantial point has to be addressed, and this is the following: The parties are aware that somewhere in July last year we discussed at that time based on the evidence available at that time a maybe outcome of the case on a consensual basis. Later on we handed down a 98 bis decision with a clear distinction between that -- what at that time the Judges thought would be the assessment of the evidence by the, at that time, working Judges and the possibility for a reasonable trial of fact. We make this clear distinction, and we uphold this clear distinction, also when the composition of the Bench was changed later on. However, it has to be made quite clear, especially under the evidence we heard during the last months, and primarily under the closing -- under the impression of the closing arguments given by the Prosecution that as it was indicated in our decision on 98 bis, of course everything is possible between, say, acquittal and that what is foreseen under the Rules and what was requested by the Prosecution. So therefore, in order not to leave open any misguidance for the Defence, the Defence should know that these possibilities still exist and a lot has changed since July last year and the 31st of October, 2002. I only wanted from a point of fairness to recall this before I give now the floor to the Defence for the closing arguments by the Defence, to hear also the other side. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning. May it please the Court. My learned colleagues from the OTP, Mr. Lukic, Dr. Stakic, good morning. Initially, I would like to express our thanks and appreciation to the Court, its staff, the Registry, the people who are involved in the entire process, including the court reporters, the translators, the personnel at the Victim and Witness Unit protection department, all of whom are vital components to securing that a trial be conducted in a professional and efficient manner. On behalf of Dr. Stakic and the entire Defence team, we thank you. I would like initially to make some preliminary remarks before I highlight some of the evidence and comments by the OTP made last Friday. This is indeed a difficult and complex case. It is difficult because in our view the OTP has exaggerated and distorted the facts in order to fulfil their mandate. It is complex because it is based entirely on circumstantial evidence, circumstantial evidence that in our view is based upon hearsay, speculation, innuendo, and conjecture. You will never hear the OTP state publicly or privately that they are satisfied with an acquittal or with a conviction which had a minor sentence so long as there was a fair trial. Instead, the OTP persists publicly and privately to obtain the only mandate that they care about, and that is conviction ratios. The goal of a conviction at any cost is plainly evident in this case and that the OTP has decided that that goal supersedes what this Court's mandate is and what the Defence professional obligations are, and that is to provide truth and bring forth the truth to the Tribunal. We can see what their mandate is by virtue of the fact witnesses that they have called, by virtue of their selection of their in-house experts, as well as by virtue of their tireless efforts in persisting to shift the burden of proof and raise irrelevant, untrue, and baseless issues only to reach their goals. The OTP fact witnesses in general, with few exceptions, were diligent in recalling extraordinary precise details, some of which at times were inconsistent with their prior statements, some of which were plainly wrong, based upon facts that we learned, some were based on hearsay testimony, and some were based on testimony and recollection which can only be classified as conjecture. Needless to say, after ten years, after the tragic events that occurred in Prijedor in the spring and summer of 1992, for those six to eight weeks, it is indeed normal, reasonable, and expected not to recall every detail precisely and accurately. What perhaps is most interesting and rather significant, that these fact witnesses offered by the Office of the Prosecution, when asked by the Court to recollect their relationships or opinions that they may have had with Dr. Stakic, remembered and unequivocally were positive, honest, and forthright. However, what is not surprising, at least to us, but is most certainly professionally troubling and disturbing is that the OTP never asked questions of their own witnesses about Dr. Stakic. We are forever grateful to the Court for asking witnesses called by the OTP about Dr. Stakic's personality, character, and reputation. In our view, the OTP had the obligation and power to put forth the truth and an obligation to put forth evidence so that there be a fair trial on the merits. We believe they failed in that. The OTP in their oral presentation strains to claim with a straight face that this is not a case against the Serbs of Prijedor, that this is not a case against the Serbs of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that it is not a case against the Serbs of Republika Srpska. I ask myself, as we all should, how many witnesses of Serbian ethnicity did the OTP call? How many of those heroes that the Office of the Prosecution now says exist who are Serbs, how many did they call? How many military men who were honourable and noble in following the rules of combat and rules of engagement did the OTP call? None. There must be a reason if we're going to offer to a Tribunal and a Court a fair and balanced view of all the facts, one would think that they would offer those witnesses, if not live, perhaps through other mechanisms as provided by the rules. Our position was not that Dr. Stakic was a hero. Our position is that Dr. Stakic is innocent. Our position is most certainly from all the evidence that we have heard that the Office of the Prosecution has failed to meet something they don't want to discuss, something never mentioned in their closing argument, that they failed to meet the burden of proof. They don't want to discuss the burden of proof not because they feel it's irrelevant but because they know when they take the evidence and apply it to the law and apply it to the standard required, that they will come up extraordinarily short. Based upon all the evidence, including the fact witnesses offered by the Office of the Prosecution, an acquittal is warranted in this case. Not once was there a discussion by the Office of the Prosecution of what weight, if any, we should give certain documents, what weight, if any, we should give to certain testimony from witnesses, what weight we should give to both documents and testimony when they're inconsistent or Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. compatible. Not once does the OTP in an honest and refreshing manner discuss the evidence that they produced that exonerates Dr. Stakic. Instead, they strike at our emotions and recall the tragic, undisputed horrific killings by criminal, barbaric and insane individuals that occurred in Prijedor. Not once did we hear from the Office of the Prosecution a discussion of the law and its application to the facts. Not once do we hear from the Office of the Prosecution the law as cited in the OTP versus Krnojelac case at paragraph 83, "Without direct evidence, a Chamber may not infer the existence of criminal mens rea unless the inference being drawn is the only reasonable inference that may be drawn from such facts." Not once did we hear the Office of the Prosecution take their theory that there was an intent to destroy Croats and particularly Muslims and apply it to see if that inference is the only reasonable inference that can be drawn. Not once, in our view, are they genuine in their application and interpretation of the facts as they were presented. We cannot and we should not, despite the OTP's desire, ignore all the fact witnesses called by both the OTP and the Defence. Those witnesses addressed Dr. Stakic's mental state, his attitude, his opinions, his views, and his mens rea, his intent prior to, during, and after the period of the fourth amended indictment, or as I prefer to call it, the fourth amended complaint, because quite frankly the difference between the two are well recognised and accepted in the law, but what we heard on Friday was just a reiteration of complaints of an opening statement of the Rule 98 bis discussion without an honest application of the law, of the burden, and of the facts in their totality. We are grateful to be have given an opportunity to present some evidence and to present our case before this Tribunal. We are not surprised that at the end of their case the OTP has abandoned their military and demographic experts and now merely rely on speculative, inconclusive theory linking the police to Dr. Stakic. Why did not the OTP with its unlimited resources ever wish to call a police expert in order to establish the truth as to whether local civilian political leaders such as Dr. Stakic have any control or authority or influence over the police? Why didn't the OTP give the police rules, regulations, and laws to their military expert so we can establish the truth and determine what, if any, authority or influence a civilian political leader such as Dr. Stakic may have over the police? I apologise, it may be a silly question. The answer, I believe, is rather obvious. The OTP did not give their military expert, Dr. Brown, the military rules, regulations, and laws. Why would they ever think about giving Dr. Brown the police rules, regulations, and laws? What is the inference that when you call a military expert to talk about purported links between the military and the civilian authorities and when you claim or complain in an indictment that there is a link between the military and the civilian authority that you don't even give the military expert the rules and regulations governing that body? Yet they complain under Article 7(3) and under the theory de jure and/or de facto that there is culpability by Dr. Stakic. Did they really not give Mr. Brown those rules and regulations? Did Mr. Brown really not understand what the rules and regulations were? If we recall his testimony, he stated on several occasions, "My remit." His remit, his job, his task as given to him, as he so tells us, by Ms. Joanna Korner of the OTP, was to look at the facts in a very narrow and in a very prejudicial manner in order to attempt to weave facts to support their complaint and indictment. And that's what Mr. Brown did. He had no choice but to do that by virtue of his employment. Mr. Koumjian seems to think that because you're on someone's payroll you must do anything and everything that they so direct when he questioned some of our witnesses and asked about payments to certain employees or to certain offices. Why can't we use their logic and reject their experts by virtue of the fact that they are prejudiced and not -- and did not give an objective summary or analysis of the facts for this Tribunal? Because that would be unfair, according to the OTP. It's unfair to use their arguments to apply to us, the Defence. It would be unfair to them for the Defence to be able to utilise documents that in one way or another would reveal the truth or raise a reasonable doubt on the issues and merits of this case. I strongly believe that the OTP had not only unlimited resources to call police experts but the inference is that they chose not to. One can counter that statement by saying, "We don't have police experts at our disposal," or perhaps one can strengthen our position to say if you will argue that there is a link between the police and Mr. Drljaca and Dr. Stakic and that your whole theory of the case is now changed, that in fact it is the relationship between the police and Dr. Stakic that is most important. Our argument is strengthened, I believe, if we can establish and show to the Court that the Prosecution had at their disposal police experts. We heard from two. Mr. Inayat and Mr. O'Donnell, they told us - we have to believe them on this - that they're very well experienced and enormously trained and were former police officers. In fact, they offered testimony on many, many facets of this case, including chain of custody, as well as the documentation that was procured once by court order, and on another occasion by the OTP without an order. Is it not important to have an expert in this case? Is it not important to have someone review the police protocol, rules, regulations, and laws? It's not important if you wish to distort the evidence. It is not important if you wish the truth not to be known. It is not important if you desire that there be no question about whether there is reasonable doubt. When viewing this case and accepting the OTP's theory that the police was linked to Dr. Stakic and therefore he is responsible for all the crimes committed by the police and its staff, one cannot escape or ignore those questions or those issues. To do so would, in my view, be a travesty. The only reasonable inference, as directed by the law, that may be drawn from the fact that the OTP refused to call a police expert, refused to produce documents relating to rules, regulations, and protocol of the police, despite the fact that they did a search and seizure, had a warrant, obtained all the documents from the police department, the only reasonable inference should favour the accused, Dr. Stakic. He does not have the burden of proof, despite the tireless efforts to shift that burden. I believe, from the limited fact witnesses that the Defence called, who discussed the issues of the police, that this Court can in fact decide the issue that there was absolutely no link, absolutely no power or authority to order or influence the police by Dr. Stakic or any of the civilian authorities. Quite honestly, the real reason the OTP did not call a police expert and the inference that should be drawn is because there is no expert anywhere, even those employed by the Office of the Prosecution, who can under oath honestly tell this Tribunal that what the Office of the Prosecution states in its indictment, argues in its oral presentation, is even remotely true. We know that if any such expert or witness existed, the OTP would have found them and he would have testified. No police expert would ever validate or accept the baseless and distorted allegations that are set forth in this indictment, in their theory against Dr. Stakic relating to the police. We ask ourselves: Where is the evidence or the rationale that the OTP claims exists that Dr. Stakic was the superior to Mr. Simo Drljaca? In fact, the evidence is rather uniform and establishes that Mr. Simo Drljaca was a subordinate to no one in Prijedor. Why ignore the fact witnesses who describe Mr. Drljaca's character, reputation, and personality? Was that an omission by the OTP in their closing argument? Should we not before this Tribunal take the evidence that perhaps is claimed to be difficult and complex and attempt to show the Tribunal how it favours one side or another? Why did the OTP ignore the fact witnesses who described Mr. Drljaca's character, reputation, and personality? Because to reach their theory and their conclusion that Mr. Drljaca was a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. subordinate to Dr. Stakic, you must ignore that evidence. But thankfully we know that you cannot, and the burden of proof on every issue in this case continues to stand with the Office of the Prosecution. Why ignore former police officers who testified and who knew Mr. Drljaca and who unequivocally said that civilian authorities had absolutely no power to direct, control, instruct, or order the police, much less the chief of police, Mr. Drljaca? Why ignore the facts that witnesses have said that Mr. Drljaca does not and would not be influenced by anyone, much less civilians, much less politicians during the spring and summer of 1992? The evidence is rather uniform and it establishes beyond a reasonable doubt that Mr. Drljaca was subordinate to no one in Prijedor. The OTP asked many questions on Friday, some rhetorical, some sarcastic, some offensive, quite frankly. They ask a question that they were surprised that Dr. Stakic's witnesses, that no one came forth to say that Dr. Stakic helped individuals in one manner or another. What they don't share with the Court is what their policy is. I'm sure we'll hear from them. In every case before this Tribunal, in every trial that has occurred thus far - and I can say with great confidence that will occur in the future - when a defendant brings forth witnesses to show either mitigation or to negate elements such as mens rea, by showing positive acts or conduct, the Office of the Prosecution has its strategy all prepared, well thought out. They don't accept that view and they don't say, "Now, this actually hurts our case. It may touch upon our burden of proof." Instead, they take the consistent position that they have to suggest if that defendant was able to assist Witness X, Y, or Z, then he must have had power and he must have been able to help others but chose not to. The real reason, Mr. Koumjian, the Defence couldn't bring witnesses to show that Dr. Stakic did something helpful or helped people during the spring and summer of 1992 is right in front of you, and that is that he had no power. He had no authority. And he was indeed unable to help anyone, even himself. The OTP claims that the Defence wants to "rewrite history." I found it offensive. I found it to be a shameful comment. But perhaps there is a misunderstanding. Perhaps they truly believe that portraying reality would be rewriting their distorted history, for all the Defence would like to do is to portray reality, show the Court what really happened, when did it really happen, why did it really happen. We would like to portray reality so that the facts in this case can be placed in their proper and honest context. What really happened? How did it really happen? Why did it really happen? These were questions that were never pursued by the Prosecution investigators in any of the statements that they took from the witnesses that they brought forth. Never do they discuss the complete economic and social deterioration due to the cries of secession. Never do they discuss the deterioration of lawfulness and why it occurred throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1991 and 1992. Never do they discuss chaos and why the military in their daily military reports uses that word often and regularly. What's interesting is when they had their military expert, Mr. Brown, testify, the Court will recall towards the close of the direct examination the Defence were offered 92 or 94 military daily reports under Rule 68 exculpatory. Yes, it was late. Yes, we accepted their apology that it was a mistake and an interoffice issue or problem. But what I find most disturbing is that the military expert did not review what the Prosecution itself calls exculpatory under Rule 68. The military expert had no interest in those documents because his "remit" was to find a link and to find what he calls under military standards coordination between the police and the military. How objective, how thorough was the analysis by their experts? We know, and much to my surprise, that the Prosecution experts are at times given second and third chances to testify. We saw it with Ms. Tabeau, or Dr. Tabeau, the demographer. She came back after being unable to fulfil questions or answer questions. We also know that the exhumation witness, Mr. Nicholas Sebire was given a second opportunity after he failed to share with us what we consider to be fundamental issues as to who was involved in the exhumations, how many exhumations did the Federation do versus the OTP alone, how many exhumations did the OTP do with the Federation? He couldn't answer basic background questions, yet this Court in all its wisdom gave him a second chance to testify, and he in fact did. The military expert, in our view, as a professional that he claims he is should have on his own requested and required that he review those 92 or so military daily reports, and he himself through the Office of the Prosecution should have applied that a supplemental report be given so that his report would truly be considered and the weight be given to it that is just. Instead, they sat silent. If the Court asked the military expert or ordered him to review those documents, I truly wonder what his results and opinions would be. The Court was kind enough to give us an opportunity and generous enough to admit those documents into evidence. I invite the Court to review all the military reports, as I'm confident that you will, and to see how the military describes the situation in Prijedor and in Bosnia and Herzegovina when they talk about lawlessness, chaos, and disorder, when they talk about the inefficiency of the civilian authorities, when they discuss that extremists, both from the Muslim, as well as the Serb ethnic side, are looting, committing crimes, burning homes, threatening people. Of course Mr. Brown doesn't want to include that in his report. It doesn't fit their mandate. It doesn't fit their theory of the case. The military reports also reveal the relationship between the police and the structures between the two organisations. The military reports also reveal when police activity was illegal and what was done to try to prevent or punish those individuals. Of course, according to the Office of the Prosecution, those things are not relevant when it comes to having their expert review and analyse and render an opinion on those topics. They only become relevant when they can argue it from baseless and unsubstantiated innuendo and speculation. Never do any of their experts discuss the Serb refugees. Never do any of their experts discuss what effect would people from another town, the influx of those individuals, what role do they play in society or in Prijedor in 1992? It's simply irrelevant. The military reports give us an insight into some of the problems associated with a mass influx of people into a town or a community. Never do we hear from the Office of the Prosecution that the horrific and tragic incidents and killings that occurred in Prijedor in the spring and summer of 1992 were caused by drunken soldiers. We heard testimony about that. Isn't it their burden of proof? Isn't it their duty to reconcile some of those issues? Isn't it their duty to address the issues found in the evidence, both the oral testimony and the military reports, when it's cited that there was vendetta, revenge, pure criminal behaviour that was the result of some of these tragic events? Shouldn't they address those issues at some point, at the very least in their oral presentation? They don't because it does not fit their mandate, it does not fit their theory of the case. They would rather sweep and argue with a broad brush than to get to the detail of the truth. Lawlessness prevailed not because of Dr. Stakic. Lawlessness prevailed in spite of Dr. Stakic and what he said and what his stood for. We must follow the general principle outlined in the decisional authority of this Tribunal. Without direct evidence, we may not infer the existence of a criminal mens rea unless the inference being drawn is the only reasonable inference that may be drawn from such facts. Was the Prosecution truly that compelling to say - although, I'm sure they stipulate and will agree - that this is a circumstantial case? So when we look at inference, the evidence that we have, is it the only reasonable inference? Is the inference they're trying to draw reasonable Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. on both when you apply the facts and when you take an objective view of the evidence? The answer will be no. Therefore, the Office of the Prosecution does not and cannot sustain their plea and complaint of a conviction against Dr. Stakic. Well, perhaps it's time to examine the facts or their facts, so I'll move away from some of my preliminary comments and address some of the facts that the OTP claim reveal that Dr. Stakic had the criminal intent, was associated with this criminal element, and committed by virtue of his association these crimes that they set forth in their complaint -- I mean, indictment. The OTP would like to Court to believe that there was a plan, a criminal plan, a joint criminal enterprise as early as 1991, wherein the Serbs, and specifically Dr. Stakic, desired, wished, and intended to - it's found on page 10 of their oral presentation last week - that Dr. Stakic intended, wished, and desired "to destroy and change forever the demographics of Prijedor." A criminal plan, they claim, whose objective was to forever change the composition of Prijedor and whose direct and sole purpose of this joint criminal enterprise was to, "Intended to destroy the Croats and particularly the Muslim communities that have become the majority of persons in Prijedor." Let's examine the evidence that they so preciously rely on. Let's examine the evidence to see if there's any truth or at the very least reasonable doubt to their theory and allegation. With the Court's permission, we would like to review Exhibit 94A -- S94A, please. Oh, it's not hooked up. We have asked the technicians, Your Honour, to assist us with a cable, but I think we may need a break at this point so that we could coordinate and have the technicians place these exhibits on the screen, as the Office of the Prosecution has done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stays adjourned until quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. And please continue with your presentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. As I was saying before the break, the OTP would like to Court to believe there was a plan, a criminal plan, a joint criminal enterprise, as early as 1991. We can view their evidence two ways: One, we can view it to determine what the truth was at the given time; and two, we can view it to determine whether it creates a substantial doubt against the theory and the burden of proof that they've alleged before this Court. When viewing these exhibits, I think the Court will find both answers in favour of Dr. Stakic. The evidence when we view it will show that there is a significant reasonable and logical inference that Dr. Stakic did not possess the criminal mens rea, that Dr. Stakic did not have any knowledge, that Dr. Stakic did not substantially contribute, and that Dr. Stakic indeed did not have any effective control over any of the criminal acts and conduct that tragically occurred in Prijedor. The joint criminal enterprise purports to have existed in 1991 by the Office of the Prosecution. They say that plan and objective, its sole purpose was "intended to destroy the Croats and particularly the Muslim communities that have become the majority of persons in Prijedor." In 1991? Should we be suspect of their theory and their allegations? Right before the break, we said we were going to review one of their exhibits that they introduced, that they rely upon, and that they once again offer during their closing arguments. But let's look at this exhibit and document with the view of what the law says. Is it the only inference, that which the Prosecution suggests? Is it the only reasonable inference, that which the Prosecution suggests, that in 1991 there was a joint criminal enterprise, a criminal plan, a plan in which Dr. Stakic was imminently involved? I believe before us we have Exhibit S94A. The purpose of this exhibit, I believe, is that the Office of the Prosecution wishes and desires ever so tirelessly to infer that because Dr. Stakic became the vice-president of the SDS on September 11th, 1991, he was purportedly aware of, at that time, of the SDS plan, criminal plan, to separate the nationalities, and being elected as the vice-president of the SDS, he agreed to such a criminal plan and therefore became a member of this joint criminal enterprise. When I reviewed this document, several questions seemed to raise their heads: Would we expect at a Serb-dominated SDS meeting of September 11th, 1992 that a prominent Muslim would also be present? No, if it's true what the OTP suggests, that this was the start of the plan and this validates that Dr. Stakic was part of this criminal plan and part of this criminal enterprise. If indeed a prominent Muslim was present, can we infer that he, too, knew of this criminal plan? According to the OTP, no, because we have a double standard. Their same logic, their same theory, would not apply. But when Dr. Stakic is present, all the negative inferences can be drawn. I suggest - and I'm confident the Court knows - we cannot and do not have a double standard. Is it logical and reasonable to infer that if a prominent Muslim was present, no such plan was contemplated or existed, at least as of September 11th, 1992? Isn't truly the only reasonable inference that if there was a mixed session during the September 11th, 1992 election of Dr. Stakic as vice-president of the SDS, that in fact this document is nothing more than an attempt to distort the true facts? Before we actually review the document that the OTP relies on to muddy Dr. Stakic, I have another question: Would we expect to see at this SDS meeting, Serb-dominated, where Dr. Stakic is elected vice-president, where purportedly this plan, criminal plan, joint criminal enterprise commenced, would we expect from the minutes of that meeting to hear and to see a discussion on the concept of unity a criminal plan, yet a discussion on the concept of unity? Would we expect -- would we expect to see at this Serb-dominated SDS meeting where Dr. Stakic was elected vice-president on September 11th, 1992 that there was a discussion, a speech, about life together is the only possible solution? How can we have those types of comments and discussions at a meeting which according to the OTP was the commencement of a joint criminal enterprise, a criminal plan, something that Dr. Stakic purportedly participated in? Isn't the only reasonable inference, if we view this document, that Dr. Stakic acquiesced to that theme, to the theme of unity, to the theme that life together is the only possible solution? Only with a vivid imagination and a distortion of the facts can we view Exhibit 94 to suggest that somehow at that time there was a plan, a criminal plan, a joint criminal enterprise. But let us clearly and honestly and objectively view Exhibit 94A and really see what the truth is. Was there a criminal plan? Was a prominent Muslim present? Was there a speech on unity? Was there a speech that had the overriding theme that life together is the only possible solution? I think we can find on that which is the last page of those minutes, which is before us on the screen -- but just so that the record is clear, it has ERN number 00916407, I believe on it -- that page 4 states, and I quote, "Professor Muhamed Cehajic, President of the Municipal Assembly, also wished to speak. He noted with pleasure the fine organisation of the Assembly session and the very well chosen entertainment. As he said, he wanted to speak because he was very pleased with Mr. Nesovic's address, which was all devoted to the concept of unity. The overriding theme of the speech was that life together is the only possible solution." What's interesting is that the Office of the Prosecution in their view deems this document to suggest something negative. Shouldn't we apply the law, the law that there is a presumption of innocence to the accused, the law which unequivocally says if an inference or presumption should be made, we should favour the presumption of innocence? This Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. document, without the presumption of innocence, clearly, only, and reasonably infers that Dr. Stakic did not and was not a participant in a plan, a criminal plan, or any such purported joint criminal enterprise. But the OTP doesn't care what the documents tell us. They only use that which is beneficial to their theory and their complaint. The Office of the Prosecution says the Serbs and every ethnic group have a right to secession, the Serbs and every ethnic group have a right to self-determination. The Serbs is not what this case is about. But when you view this document, you must ask yourself: Are they saying Dr. Stakic was a bad and evil man because he became vice-president of the SDS? Was Dr. Stakic evil because he participated in an assembly which spoke of unity and life together as the only possible solution? Shouldn't that be the only reasonable and logical inference we can draw from the exhibit that they use in their closing argument and in their case in chief? Why didn't they address this and call it a non sequitur if they truly believe it has no relevance? This document, September 1991, can only reasonably infer that Dr. Stakic agreed with the speech of unity and the speech of togetherness between all ethnic citizens of Prijedor. Now, the Office of the Prosecution seems to suggest that Dr. Stakic should have done more. In life, when we reflect, we all should and certainly could do more. That's not the criminal standard. Did Dr. Stakic ever speak of peace? Did Dr. Stakic ever say he is against the war? Did Dr. Stakic ever say that problems should be solved in a peaceful manner? If he said it, I'm sure that the Office of the Prosecution would have grabbed those facts and they would have told us why they were unimportant, or they would have told us why they are of no significance. Instead - and I submit to the Court - Dr. Stakic did, in fact, speak of peace; Dr. Stakic did say he was against the war; Dr. Stakic did say that problems should be resolved in a peaceful manner. The Office of the Prosecution chose to ignore those facts. Instead, they'd like to muddy the waters. They move in their argument after suggesting that it's bad, although not anti-Serb, but it's bad to be a member of the SDS and it's terrible that Dr. Stakic became vice-president of the SDS in September of 1991. Despite the facts that we saw, that there was discussions and speeches of unity and life togetherness, we move the film and the story a little closer to the indictment. January 1992, the Office of the Prosecution contends that at that time, January 7th, 1992, the Serbs and Dr. Stakic formed a parallel government, formed a parallel municipal assembly in Prijedor. Is that the joint criminal enterprise? Was that a criminal plan? Would it surprise us that in January 1992 that the formation of this Serb-parallel government was made public, was publicised in the newspaper, in the radio, and was known throughout Prijedor? Does that mean everyone in the town knew of this joint criminal enterprise, of this criminal plan? Did Dr. Stakic at that interview or those interviews offered by the Office of the Prosecution to show a parallel government, did he speak of war? Did he deceive the Serbs? Did he tell the Serbs that the Muslims were going to attack them? Did Dr. Stakic speak of peace or did he speak of destroying Croats, Muslims, and other non-Serbs in Prijedor? Well, let's take an honest look at the evidence and apply it to the law, that circumstantial evidence, that hearsay evidence which the Office of the Prosecution relies on to suggest that there was a plan. 6A, their exhibit, 6A, in our view unequivocally, without doubt, finds and infers that we can conclude Dr. Stakic was not a participant in a purported criminal plan, was not a member of a purported joint criminal enterprise. The exhibit Your Honours are now reviewing is S6A. If I can just have the top again, please. The top obviously shows that it's an article from Kozarski Vjesnik dated the 31st of January, 1992. It's publicised, the fact that the Serbs had a parallel government in January 1992 is publicised. What's the inference of that? That there was a secret criminal plan? If it was made public, does it not mean that all ethnic groups knew of this criminal plan, or is it indeed logical and reasonable to infer and conclude that the formation of this parallel government was not criminal at all? Nevertheless, let's assume for a moment that we are inclined to infer evidence in favour of the Office of the Prosecution, even though that's not the law, which I also submit is not only not the law; it's wrong and it's erroneous, since the law is rather clear, that if more than one reasonable inference may be drawn, the facts should - and we submit must - be made in favour of the accused. The presumption of innocence overrides such dual reasonable inferences. Would you expect in this document that the OTP relies upon to show a joint criminal enterprise, a criminal plan? Would you expect to learn Dr. Stakic spoke publicly about it, that Dr. Stakic when asked on the 31st of January, 1992 about this formation of a new parallel government, when asked, "How is it possible to divide territory, the present municipality of Prijedor, especially the town of Prijedor, and its ethnically mixed villages and hamlets?" Let's look at the answer. And I think and dare say that you'll find Dr. Stakic was optimistic, that the SDS and the SDA could and would work out their problems. Dr. Stakic felt, he was of the mindset -- he was of the mindset as of January 31st, 1992 that if there was a problem with the SDA that could not be resolved, the establishment of a Serb municipality would be done in a peaceful and civilised manner. I think if we turn to the second page, the Court will find that question and that answer in the fifth paragraph, if you count from the bottom of the page, or the second paragraph from the top. Is question is designated with a dot, and the paragraph is designated with a slash. Dr. Stakic, a member of a joint criminal enterprise? Dr. Stakic, participating in a criminal plan? Dr. Stakic, inflaming the Serbs in Prijedor according to the Office of the Prosecution? Here he is at the height of what the Office of the Prosecution calls an ambitious career, recently elected the vice-president of the SDS, now a member of a parallel Serb government in Prijedor. What better opportunity than to tell everyone through the papers what he feels and what he thinks and what his intentions are. It's right before us. Not only in September of 1991 but in January 1992 Dr. Stakic speaks of resolution, negotiation "in a peaceful and civilised manner." We must ask ourselves, since the Office of the Prosecution didn't: That fact, how do we apply it to the law? Is the only reasonable inference that Dr. Stakic possesses the criminal mens rea? Does this fact not unequivocally show that indeed Dr. Stakic was not at any time a member of a joint criminal enterprise and did not possess any criminal intent to any of the citizens in the Prijedor municipality at any time? The journalist asks another question that follows immediately thereafter. The Office of the Prosecution seems to suggest that Dr. Stakic should have done more, he gave negative speeches. We'll address some of those speeches later, where they talk about the jihad and the holy war. But let's talk about these first, which were conveniently omitted from the argument. Does Dr. Stakic talk about the prevention of war? Let's look at his answer on the 31st of January, 1992. He states in the last sentence on the last paragraph of page 2 of Exhibit 6A, "The SDS is aware of the fact and will use all possible arguments and its own reputation to prevent war from ensuing but rather, for problems to be solved in a peaceful manner." Is it really truly the honest position of the Office of the Prosecution that Dr. Stakic was a member of a joint criminal enterprise and possessed a criminal plan as of September and January 1992? What evidence, other than to say that he became a member of the SDS and that the Serbs formed a parallel government in Prijedor, do they have? Does membership in a party allow us to only reasonably infer a criminal plan? Does the formation, the public formation of a parallel government in January 1992 honestly allow us to reasonably infer that it was a criminal Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. plan? When we look at what Dr. Stakic said and what others said at those two instances, if they spoke of criminal activity, if they spoke of "destroying Croats and particularly Muslims," perhaps and indeed an argument could be made for such a theory, but those aren't the facts. The facts are plain. They're obvious. They are before us, even though the Prosecution ignores them. Can the only reasonable inference be that when they speak of unity and Dr. Stakic is present, when Dr. Stakic speaks of preventing war and working together in a peaceful manner, should not -- not only the inference be but I think it's unquestionably a fact that Dr. Stakic did not possess any criminal intent for any of the tragedies that occurred in Prijedor in 1992. We have extrinsic evidence, documents that we review about events and Dr. Stakic's state of mind, his mens rea, before the events of April 1992. The OTP chose to ignore those, but they do not stop there. They persist in their tireless effort to scan the evidence without due diligence and without detail. If they were truthful and honest, they would have raised these issues when they presented these facts, and they would have told the Court that in fact the reasonable inference that someone is a member of a party without doubt renders that person to be criminal. But they can't, because that's not true. What they chose to do is to hide and shy away from the truth, the truth of what Dr. Stakic's mens rea, intent, opinions, and views were of all the citizens of Prijedor in September and January 1992. But they ignore the documentary evidence, and then they proceed to ignore the live evidence, the fact witnesses. Did the Defence not bring one witness that knew Dr. Stakic before the events of April 30th, 1992? Did the Defence bring not more than one witness to discuss the events prior to April of 1992? Ignore those facts, because the Office of the Prosecution is telling you you must ignore those facts if you want to acquit. We cannot ignore the September 11th extrinsic evidence or the January 31st extrinsic evidence. We cannot ignore the fact witnesses which discussed at length Dr. Stakic's personality, character, and reputation before April 30th, 1992. An honest discussion and an intellectually refreshing discussion would have been to talk about those issues and to confront those issues, to discuss those issues and then to argue why they should be considered or ignored, as they prefer. What did some of their witnesses say about Dr. Stakic before April 30th, 1992? Nijaz Kapetanovic, he states, "Dr. Stakic did not show or display intolerance towards people, did not." Forget about the Defence witnesses. Shouldn't they at least address their own evidence, their own witnesses, if they're going to make a claim like they do that as early as 1991 Dr. Stakic possessed a criminal plan, was part of a criminal plan, part of a joint criminal enterprise? Should we dismiss Mr. Kapetanovic and his testimony in its entirety? Should we reasonably infer that Mr. Kapetanovic was accurate and honest when he said that Dr. Stakic did not show or display intolerance towards people? What does that statement do if you apply the law and if you ask yourselves: Is that the only reasonable inference that in fact Dr. Stakic is innocent of the crimes that are alleged against him? What about that 29-year-old, Dr. Mujadzic, who the Prosecution addressed in their closing arguments, addressed Dr. Mujadzic when he stopped the Office of the Prosecution during his evidence and he says, "I never said that Dr. Stakic personally attempted to undermine tolerance in the area." What's the inference there? Should we ignore all the OTP factual evidence? I think not. I think the OTP would rather the Court ignore all the exculpatory evidence, all the favourable evidence, all the evidence that exonerates Dr. Stakic. The truth of the matter is that the burden is not ours to prove that Dr. Stakic is innocent. The truth of the matter is that if you apply the facts objectively, that you will find in favour of Dr. Stakic, that the OTP did not meet their burden of proof. What should we infer from now both the documents and the fact witnesses about Dr. Stakic? That Dr. Stakic was part of a criminal plan, as the OTP vaguely alleges, or that Dr. Stakic, as supported by the evidence, both the extrinsic and the live testimony, was not part of a criminal plan and certainly knew nothing of such a plan and in fact Dr. Stakic advocated and promoted peace and tolerance? Does this evidence really portray reality? Does this evidence really show Dr. Stakic deceiving Serbs, telling Serbs they are in danger? What an extraordinary imagination one must have in order to reach that conclusion. Let us briefly examine the period of the indictment and review some of the documents that the Office of the Prosecution relies on. And likewise, I'm going to examine some of the documents and some of the testimony that they chose to ignore because in order to portray reality, in order to make an objective assessment, a fair assessment, we should look at all the evidence collectively and examine all the evidence and then weigh that evidence. It's another issue the Office of the Prosecution didn't dare discuss. They don't discuss the burden of proof because they have not met the burden of proof. They have met and have established that many, many, thousands of people were killed in Prijedor. What's interested is that they don't remind the Court that the Defence from the beginning of this case at the direction and instruction of Dr. Stakic absolutely chose not to contest that issue and that fact. Numerous 92 bis witnesses were called from various hamlets and villages of Prijedor which discussed crimes and the brutality in which they were victimised. It's not an issue and it is not a dispute and the Defence does not contest the tragedy that fell on Prijedor in the spring and summer of 1992. We do take exception to the Office of the Prosecution attempting to strike at our emotions and to blame Dr. Stakic for those crimes, crimes that their very own fact witnesses when discussing did not, could not, and in their deepest hearts would never accuse Dr. Stakic of. Many of those victims who testified, it would have been understandable sitting in this docket to say, "This man is responsible." Those brave people, those people who suffered and continue to suffer, chose instead to tell the truth and to share with us that Dr. Stakic not only did not commit those crimes, is not responsible for those crime, was not a participant in any purported joint criminal enterprise or criminal plan resulting in those crimes from occurring. According to the OTP, after the takeover on April 30th, 1992, Dr. Stakic continued to be a member of a joint criminal enterprise with its sole objective and purpose "intending to destroy the Croat and particularly Muslim communities in Prijedor." We heard evidence from the witnesses about Dr. Stakic's feelings before April 30th, 1992. We saw concrete evidence about whether or not Dr. Stakic spoke of destruction, as they claim, or of peace and tolerance. Now, let's examine what, if anything, Dr. Stakic said after April 30th, 1992. Would it surprise us that if Dr. Stakic said, "Peace must be maintained at all costs," that the Office of the Prosecution chose to ignore that? Why would Dr. Stakic say "peace must be maintained at all costs" at an SDS meeting? Why, there is no evidence of Dr. Stakic saying anything remotely close to being negative, discriminatory, or offensive against the Muslims and Croats during that period. What a perfect forum -- what a perfect forum, May 9th, 1992, one week or so, ten days after assuming power in the Prijedor Municipality, what a perfect forum for Dr. Stakic, who just took over power, who was the vice-president of the SDS, who became the new president of the municipal assembly, what a perfect forum for Dr. Stakic. Why not rally the troops and say, "Let's expel, drive out," or as the Office of the Prosecution states "destroy" the Croat and Muslims? May 9th, at an SDS meeting, does Dr. Stakic say one single derogatory word against any ethnic group? Not one single negative comment, not one single discriminatory comment. If there was a criminal plan, why on the 9th of May, 1992 is Dr. Stakic speaking of peace? Is it not reasonable and logical to infer and to conclude that Dr. Stakic is not guilty of the crimes alleged against him, that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Dr. Stakic is not guilty of being part of a plan, criminal plan, or joint criminal enterprise? The Office of the Prosecution referenced this exhibit and discusses it, but I think that which Dr. Stakic doesn't say also is important to rebut, contradict, and to show that in fact there is reasonable doubt in the Office of the Prosecution's theory. What better forum than May 9th, 1992 for Dr. Stakic not to have used discriminatory, derogatory, and negative comments against his fellow citizens? The inference should be because Dr. Stakic did not use discriminatory, derogatory, and negative comments, that he does not possess the criminal mens rea necessary to convict him of the crimes that the Prosecution alleges. But we have more: Dr. Stakic affirmatively at that May 9th, 1992 meeting, which presumably was attended predominantly by Serbs, he states on page 2, which I think you have before you, under his name, the second paragraph, "Peace must be maintained at all costs." Is that not significant? Is that, as the Office of the Prosecution contends, irrelevant? Should we ignore it? Could we ignore it? Only if you want to convict. Only if you want to deny the truth from being presented. Only can we accept their theory and ignore such evidence, as compelling it is, if we do not and will not accept the truth and justice to prevail. Dr. Stakic at that time, according to the Office of the Prosecutor, was extremely ambitious, desiring to continue to climb the ladder. At that stage we see SK46, wherein Dr. Stakic, having been elected as vice-president, speaks of peace and tolerance. We have the January 1992 document which addresses his views on this parallel government and how the SDS and the SDA should and in his optimistic view will work things out and his statement that they will work in a peaceful and civilised manner. Ignore all the evidence. Ignore all the evidence would be a travesty of justice. Ignoring all the evidence is the only way one can conclude that the Prosecution has met their burden of proof. The weight of a document has taken up some significant time in this -- during this trial. The Office of the Prosecution doesn't assess the weight of any of their documents. We'll address some a little bit later this afternoon. But this particular document, SK46, should be given great weight and in my view heavy weight. Why? Out of all the documents that we reviewed, out of all the documents that they submitted, out of all the documents that they distorted in their opinion as to what they purport to represent, Mr. Robert Donia with respect to this document specifically was asked on his testimony of the 24th of April, 2002, page 2165, specifically lines 8 through 10, in discussing SK46, question: "Is there any reason, sir, that we should doubt the veracity of the person reporting these notes as they being attributed to Dr. Stakic?" Answer: "No." Even their expert, even their witnesses, acknowledge that there is no doubt whatsoever that Dr. Stakic said those words, intended those words, and was of the opinion at all times that peace must be maintained at all costs. I'd like to address another document that's in existence, and that is document S200. And until we get that document up. I asked on SK46, why does the OTP ignore the substance of that document? How does the OTP reconcile that document and those words with their theory that Dr. Stakic is part of a joint criminal enterprise? How could they on one hand say that Dr. Stakic was an advocate of war, namely deceiving the Serbs, telling the Serbs that there was going to be some tragedy to fall upon them, and on the other hand, publicly and in private meetings with all Serbs being present, to suggest, to affirmatively state peace must be maintained at all costs? That was May 9th, 1992. One week later, May 16th, 1992, there was a 50th year jubilee anniversary for Prijedor. It's cited in a newspaper article reflected under S200. Dr. Stakic at that jubilee anniversary speaks, one week after his comment that peace must be maintained at all costs. One week later, and approximately three weeks into his new government where he's the president of the municipality, 16 days exactly, would we expect Dr. Stakic to say at that time, if anything the OTP says about him is true, that at that time he would be banging the drums of war, he would be talking about hate, intolerance, and the need for separation? Did Dr. Stakic use that word "destroy" at any time for his fellow Muslims and Croats and non-Serbs? The document you're looking at merely provides us with a backdrop of what the evidence really says. That confirms that there was a jubilee celebration on or about the 16th of May, 1992. At that event I am telling the Court that Dr. Stakic said that Prijedor will be an oasis for peace and nothing ugly will happen in Prijedor. I say it. I think the Court might be suspect and tell me, "Well, you can't offer it without a factual basis, and S200 doesn't seem to suggest it." That same standard should be applied to my learned colleagues. When they say it, they should back it up. When they make an allegation or an assertion, it cannot and should not be baseless and without foundation. Dr. Stakic did say on May 16th, 1992 in front of hundreds and thousands of people that Prijedor will be an oasis for peace and that nothing ugly would happen in Prijedor. How do we know that? Because I said it was so? No. We have it, if we honestly look at the evidence that the OTP would like to ignore. Witness Z, who testified for the Office of the Prosecution, when Ms. Sutherland was asking her questions, she admitted to that, the witness, Witness Z. There was nothing to admit. She offered it as a conscious recollection of Dr. Stakic who stood before her criminally accused. She could have forgotten about that statement. She could have avoided making that statement, or she could have ignored the statement, as the Office of the Prosecution does. Instead, this honourable person, this honest individual, having given an oath to tell the truth, told us the truth. Here's what she says: Witness Z, page 7538, line 21, in part of her answer, "He," Dr. Stakic, "said that Prijedor would be an oasis of peace, that nothing ugly would happen in Prijedor, nothing like that had happened in other parts of Bosnia, for example, in Foca." This witness in her testimony, I think the Court will find when reviewing it, look at Exhibit S200. She confirmed she went to that celebratory 50th anniversary jubilee meeting. She confirmed Dr. Stakic said that. So what do we have? If I'm the Prosecution, I would tell the Court, "Yes, in May -- May 19th, 1992, Dr. Stakic speaks of peace. May 16th, 1992 he tells the citizens of Prijedor that Prijedor will be an oasis for peace, nothing ugly would happen there." Be forthright with the evidence. Be objective with the factual evidence that is undisputed so that we can make an honest and refreshing assessment as to what inferences, reasonable or not, that we can make. Is it reasonably with this backdrop of the May 19th, 1992 speech by Dr. Stakic, the May 16th, 1992 speech by Dr. Stakic, when he's at what the Prosecution calls the height of his overachieving career, does that infer criminal intent? Does that infer criminal conduct? Does that infer that Dr. Stakic was inflaming the passions of the Serbs by telling them that terrible things would happen to them? Peace, terrible? Tolerance, terrible? Only with an extraordinary imagination could one conclude such a preposterous and completely biased view. That is Dr. Stakic's intent. That was Dr. Stakic's intent during the period of the indictment, and the evidence proves it. The evidence proves what his intent was before as well as during the period of the indictment. Oasis of peace? Peace must be maintained at all costs. May 16th and May 9th respectfully. That, Your Honours, was Dr. Stakic's goal, peace to be maintained at all costs, Prijedor to be an oasis of peace. That, Your Honours, was Dr. Stakic's plan. Peace at all costs and Prijedor to be an oasis of peace. That, Your Honour, was Dr. Stakic's mens rea. Peace, not violence, will prevail. Good, and not ugly, will prevail. Regrettably, as we heard from the citizens of Prijedor themselves, Dr. Stakic's wishes, desires, and intent did not prevail. The criminal behaviour of drunken soldiers, of criminal individuals, whether it be for Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. revenge, vendetta, or pure spite, was far too uncontrollable for anyone, much less Dr. Stakic. Now, those first three or so weeks that Dr. -- when Dr. Stakic took over power and advocated peace, did we have any crime, did we have any killings? Did we maintain to the extent that it was possible that things proceed in a normal manner? There was no evidence whatsoever to suggest that during those first three weeks that Dr. Stakic was involved in any criminal activity, was part of any criminal activity, or was a member of a joint criminal enterprise that purported to possess criminal intent. What changed? We do not want to recreate history. We want a portrayal of reality and the truth. What occurred was that there was an attack on Serb soldiers who were passing at a checkpoint at Hambarine on May 22nd, 1992. The Office of the Prosecution admits and acknowledged they were not there and they tell us they don't know what truly happened, but they share with us, again, what they think the evidence reasonably infers. They tell us that the Defence, having brought Witness DH, who was a military man and who passed through that checkpoint at Hambarine that morning, that that proves that the members of that checkpoint were reasonable, were never going to attack or harm anyone because DH passed through there in a military uniform unharmed. Is it reasonable to infer that since Witness DH was of the Croatian ethnic background that, he passed relatively freely at that checkpoint? Is it reasonable to infer that the soldiers who were killed and wounded at that checkpoint were killed and wounded because they were Serbs and for no other reason? How does the Office of the Prosecution reconcile the fact that two other members of that group who were Croatian were not killed, were not injured, and are still alive and can testify, if called, to tell us what the truth is? Look at the military reports, at the conversation and the investigation that the military did as to who shot whom and why. Their expert doesn't review it because it doesn't fit into the Prosecution's theory. The Prosecution ignores it because they can only get a conviction if they ignore and distort the evidence. The fact of the matter remains that it's irrelevant who initiated or provoked the confrontation at Hambarine. The fact of the matter is that on May 22nd, 1992 there was an escalation and a complete change of events for the municipality of Prijedor as a result of that incident and those killings. Portrayal of reality. Why is it not significant from a military standpoint to discuss that on May 3rd, 1992 in the capital of Sarajevo JNA military personnel and convoy were attacked and summarily assassinated while departing their barracks? No one is trying to recreate history. That's a fact. That's an important fact that's within the period of indictment. In Tuzla, similarly, we find from Major General Lewis MacKenzie in his diary that he reports 150 Serb soldiers were attacked by Muslims at a checkpoint, were killed. Another 150 were wounded, and 300 were captured. Why is that irrelevant? Why is that recreating history? Those are facts which when you place in front of a military soldier or a military personnel that are extraordinary, that will heighten their awareness, that will indeed regrettably in Prijedor exacerbate the response to any attack to their personnel. Why do we ignore it? Because it doesn't fit into the Prosecution's theory to convict. This Court should not and must not ignore facts that are pertinent, facts that will share with us what the true intent was of the military at that time in Prijedor when they responded to the killing of their personnel, both at Hambarine and at Kozarac, as well as in the city town of Prijedor in May of 1992. The Office of the Prosecution seems to suggest that the Serbian army used as a pretext this incident at Hambarine. Wouldn't logic and reasonableness tell us that after April 30th of 1992, when the Serbs took over power, they needed no more pretext than the attack on the military in Sarajevo, the attack on the military in Tuzla in order to render any kind of response if they so desired to the non-Serbs in Prijedor? Hambarine was not a pretext. Hambarine was an unfortunate incident, a terrible provocation, and a terrible event that started the deterioration of the entire Prijedor municipality of any peacefulness and lawlessness that was desired and intended by Dr. Stakic. At what point, we must ask us -- we must ask ourselves, do we lose control? At what point was peace no longer an option for the military? For the military peace was not longer an option, I suggest, after May 30th, 1992. If Hambarine was a pretext, as the Office of the Prosecution alleges, why not at Hambarine kill everyone? Why not destroy the hundreds of homes in Hambarine? Why not, since Hambarine is in the Brdo region, continue if you had this joint criminal plan, and continue to "destroy the Croat and Muslim communities"? Why stop at the road where the barricade and roadblock was? Why stop there? Why effectively arrest no one? Why effectively kill no one? Why effectively detain no one? Because there was no joint criminal enterprise, because there was no joint criminal plan. Dr. Stakic certainly didn't know what would happen or what would result following the incident at Hambarine. The experts, I think, agreed that an ultimatum was given, that the ultimatum was proper. If according to the OTP Mr. Mujadzic was right, that there should have been an investigation, why, then, didn't Mr. Aliskovic turn himself in? Why, then, didn't the perpetrators of those criminal acts and killings turn themselves in? The checkpoint at Hambarine is a significant, an enormously important, start of what became an uncontrollable, sporadic, and inconsistent criminal behaviour throughout Prijedor. No one could anticipate Hambarine from happening, despite the fact that there were many bunkers, as the OTP says in their closing argument, many roadblocks, and many barricades throughout the Prijedor municipality. No one can anticipate that soldiers would be attacked, killed. No one can stop the military from responding to that provocation. I think, Your Honour, if I may, this would been an appropriate time for a break, with the Court's permission, of course.
