utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: 21. S235-21. Was the back side photocopied? Are we giving a fair trial to the accused? Are we trying to put forth the truth or are we in a subtle way clearly clouding the issues so that our mandate of a conviction can be upheld? This example and the others that I tried to share with the Court speaks rather clearly as to how the Court should view the Office of the Prosecution, their tactics, regretfully the evidence that they produce, specifically the evidence that they refuse to produce when asked by the Defence. The experts, including Mr. O'Donnell, who by his own words is a professional, a police officer, knowing full well what a courtroom is, what a trial is, knowing full well what his obligations are as a member of the Prosecution team, to distort that evidence, to distort this Trial Chamber, to mislead all of us is a clear sign of the confidence that they have in the portrayal of reality as to what occurred in the spring and summer of 1992 as it relates to Dr. Stakic. They cannot prevail if they follow the law. They cannot prevail if they give us an honest and objective assessment of the evidence, not a selective group of documents, but a complete set of documents. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Thank you, Madam Usher. To have force and validity, the inference - thank you very much - cannot be purely arbitrary, unreasonable, and unnatural. The circumstantial case that the Prosecution has against Dr. Stakic is completely arbitrary; it's completely unreasonable, and it's completely unnatural. At no time does the Office of the Prosecution address the issues that the Court invited us to discuss: Natural and foreseeable, substantial contribution, effective control. Can you have genocidal intent be inferred from the presumption of the evidence? Imagine that. A four-fold application to find a conviction for a crime of all crimes, genocide. Does the Prosecution address that there is absolutely no way that a conviction can be held if we presume facts that in our view are suspect, unsubstantiated, and then can we infer or make an inference, and it must be the only reasonable inference from those presumptive facts, to reach a conclusion. I respectfully submit to this Court that is not the standard, that is not the law. Jurisdictions throughout the world would not, with all due respect, accept that a standard which relies upon suspect evidence in order for it to pass muster, there must be wide and broad presumptions made in their application, and then ultimately, there must be yet another subjective, unnatural, arbitrary, and unreasonable analysis to find that the inference is the only reasonable inference from those facts. The law is not something that the Office of the Prosecution would like to discuss, because the law would find Dr. Stakic innocent of the crimes alleged. The Office of the Prosecution doesn't discuss the facts of the Room 3 massacre and how that is not a natural and foreseeable event. The Court was genuine and honest with us and informed us that it was having trouble with that event. Let's ignore it. Let's ignore all the stuff that may help Dr. Stakic. Instead, hopefully, if we tell them that as with most genocides, the first thing that happens is that you disarm the victims, and maybe if we victimise this case and tell the Court repeatedly that there was a horrific, a terrible tragedy that occurred, multiple, multiple massacres and deaths, that they were sporadic, they were uncontrollable, and they were random. I, too, if I were the Prosecution and if I had an extraordinary imagination would not want to address those issues. I believe in circumstantial cases, which are derived from hearsay, suspect documents, innuendo, would forever change the fundamental principles of law and justice. We cannot, we respectfully should not, accept the Office of the Prosecution's view of history, view of adversarial proceedings, and view of what they deem to be the truth. Justice demands more, and it demands a strict adherence to the laws. It demands all of us to strictly adhere to the fundamental principles of justice and the presumption of innocence. It demands that we strictly apply, unfortunately to the detriment to the Office of the Prosecution, the burden of proof beyond a reasonable doubt. It does not at any time suggest that that burden should be shifted or that burden to be reduced because of the magnitude of killings or the tragedy that obviously existed in Prijedor in 1992. The Office of the Prosecution fails to examine the evidence in its totality. Cumulatively, they failed in my view to analyse that evidence in a concrete manner. I believe that it is an intentional refusal to examine that evidence. Did they tell this Court that in all those, when they say "as in most genocides" - and thankfully they're wrong on that - did they tell this Court that there is not one case and logic and common sense dictate there will never be a case where a man will be charged and found guilty of genocide when he made comments on the 11th of September, on the 16th of July, on the 9th of May, on the 16th of May involving peace, tolerance, an attempt to reconcile, an attempt to work together? The goal of Dr. Stakic was undoubtedly peace based upon the evidence. There's no inference we should draw from that evidence; that is a fact. The inference the OTP would like to draw is the opposite. We don't have presumptions and inferences on undisputed facts. The fact that Dr. Stakic said "Prijedor will be an oasis of peace" on the 16th of May, 1992. That's an undisputed fact. No inference should be drawn from that fact other than to acquit. No case in any country at any time in the history of the world would ever find a gentleman like Dr. Stakic who promoted peace and tolerance during a most terrible time, the spring and summer of 1992, guilty of the crimes that are alleged. I do believe that it is reasonable, logical, and plausible that it is difficult in light of all the killings, in light of all the victims, in light of all the suffering, that we do have some reservations, that we do look at this and must ask the question "the poor people of Prijedor, the poor victims of Prijedor." I, too, feel that. However, our mandate here is not to try to lessen the pain or to lessen that unfortunate suffering. Our mandate is to analyse the facts, to analyse the documents, to analyse the testimony and determine, (a), whether the Office of the Prosecution met their burden of proof of beyond a reasonable doubt; and (b), whether Dr. Stakic, a man who promoted peace and tolerance during the time period of this criminal plan and joint criminal enterprise, should be convicted. I submit to the Court that if you view the evidence as I am confident you will honestly and objectively, that you will find in favour of Dr. Stakic and acquit Dr. Stakic of all the crimes alleged in the fourth amended indictment. Thank you, Your Honours.
